President Donald Trump on Thursday celebrated wins for the U.S. chip industry, praising Nvidia Corp.‘s (NASDAQ:NVDA) robust revenue guidance following strong second-quarter results and Micron Technology Inc.‘s (NASDAQ:MU) new $10 billion research investment as proof that his policies are drawing in trillions in domestic investment.

Congratulates Jensen Huang On Nvidia’s Numbers

Trump praised Nvidia’s results in a post on Truth Social, calling them “incredible numbers,” and added, “Congratulations to Jensen Huang… Only in America!”

The company posted second-quarter revenue of $96.22 billion, up 106% from a year earlier, alongside third-quarter guidance of $108 billion, a figure that would represent roughly 1,730% revenue growth over four years, and fiscal 2028 revenue growth guidance of 70%.

Read Also: Marvell Technology, IREN, Rubrik, Affirm Holdings and Strategy: Why These 5 Stocks Are on Investors' Radars Today

Trump Says Micron Is Bringing Critical Technology Back to the US

In a separate post, Trump called Micron one of the “hottest” companies in the world, celebrating its new $10 billion investment in research labs on top of the company’s earlier $250 billion commitment to U.S. manufacturing.

“They are keeping us at the absolute forefront of A.I. and Advanced Computing,” Trump said, adding that “combined with their previous tremendous 250 billion dollar commitment, they are creating tens of thousands of great American jobs.”

Earlier this month, the chipmaker announced the Micron Research Labs, a U.S.-based hub anchored by a flagship campus in Boise, Idaho, focused on advancing memory and AI technologies over the next decade.

“I have made it clear that America will lead the way to a new Golden Age of Science,” Trump added.

Tariff Uncertainty Looms Over the Industry

The praise comes as the Trump administration considers new semiconductor tariffs that could extend to laptops, gaming consoles, and data center servers, POLITICO reported on Thursday.

Tech companies have started lobbying against the proposal, warning it could raise costs and slow the AI data center buildout.

Micron is currently the only U.S.-based manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, a component the administration has framed as central to domestic AI supply chain security.

Trump’s Broader Stock Activity in Both Companies

Trump’s earlier disclosure, filed in May, showed more than a dozen separate Nvidia transactions during the first quarter of 2026, including purchases and sales ranging from $1,001 to $1 million, along with several Micron purchases ranging from $1,001 to $250,000.

In his most recent disclosure earlier this month, he sold between $15,001 and $50,000 of Nvidia stock on June 23, with no Micron transactions reported during that period.

Jung said, “The United States is the epicenter of AI innovation, bringing together premier customers, top-tier R&D capabilities, and partners, and the Indiana fab will become a gateway to deliver first Made in USA HBM products.”

According to Counterpoint Research, SK Hynix held 58% of the global HBM market by revenue in the first quarter of 2026, outpacing Samsung Electronics and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU), each at 21%.

Nvidia, a major SK Hynix customer, forecast a 70% jump in revenue for the next fiscal year, reinforcing confidence in sustained AI-chip demand and supporting Kwak’s view that the memory upcycle has room to run.

The U.S. government supported the project with $458 million in CHIPS Act grants and up to $500 million in loans, with the funding finalized in December 2024.

“The Big Short” investor Michael Burry is escalating his ongoing clash with Nvidia Corp.‘s (NASDAQ:NVDA) leadership, firing back at CEO Jensen Huang by pointing to the chipmaker’s latest 10-Q filing as evidence supporting his concerns over circular financing.

Spotlighting Nvidia’s agreement to guarantee billions for an OpenAI data center, Burry accused the market of ignoring clear red flags, warning that investors are “Whistling past the graveyard.”

What NVDA’s 10-Q States

The conflict reignited after Burry shared an analysis of Nvidia’s newly released second-quarter 10-Q document, highlighting the mechanics of the sector’s financing model.

The filing formally disclosed Nvidia’s agreement with SoftBank’s SB Energy for an OpenAI-leased data center. According to the 10-Q, Nvidia has entered into guarantees, “capped at a total of $105 billion,” to provide credit support for a land, power, and shell buildout on behalf of OpenAI at SB Energy’s PORTS Technology Campus in Ohio.

The filing notes that the campus involves leases for “approximately 4.25 gigawatts of IT load” and will “exclusively host NVIDIA AI infrastructure.” Pointing to these massive commitments as evidence of a self-reinforcing financial loop, Burry offered a stark four-word warning: “Whistling past the graveyard.”

Read Also: Michael Burry Says NVDA Stock Appears ‘Wildly Undervalued’ on Paper After Blowout Q2 Earnings, but Warns Nvidia Shares Are Still ‘Treading Water’

NVDA Management Downplays Circular Financing Concerns

Burry’s attack directly challenges Nvidia management, who aggressively defended their balance sheet strategy during their latest earnings call. Addressing the massive OpenAI guarantees, executives pushed back against critics alleging the company is simply funding its own demand.

CFO Colette Kress directly tackled the controversy during her prepared remarks. “We recognize the scale of this support, and we know some will call this circular financing. We see it differently.”

Huang was equally resolute in dismissing the idea that these private credit deals artificially inflate revenue. Defending the Ohio project, Huang stated, “No. OpenAI will pay the lease.”

The Bear vs. The Bull

While Huang frames the massive capital deployment as a necessary masterstroke to secure infrastructure for frontier AI labs that are outgrowing their credit profiles, Burry remains deeply skeptical.

Even after buying December Nvidia call options as a hedge against his bearish position, Burry maintains a massive short position against the broader AI ecosystem, insisting that the mechanics revealed in the 10-Q validate his long-term bearish thesis.

How Has Nvidia Performed in 2026?

At the last check, the NVDA stock was trading 0.64% lower in overnight trading. It was up 22.24% year-to-date, advanced by 25.54% over the last year, and rose 28.66% over the last six months. It closed 8.74% higher at $227.98 per share on Thursday.

Companies closely aligned with President Donald Trump are reportedly seeking stronger ties with Democrats ahead of the midterm elections, preparing for a possible shift in House control.

Companies such as Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) are making substantial donations to Democrats, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal, as they seek to hedge against a potential change in congressional power after previously backing Trump and Republican initiatives.

Other companies, including Paramount Skydance (NASDAQ:PSKY) and Kalshi, are hiring former Democratic aides to bolster their government relations strategies, the report added.

Big tech companies, especially those that played a major role in Trump’s political campaign in 2024 and signature projects like the ballroom, are reportedly forming internal task forces to prepare for potential congressional and criminal investigations.

Companies like Meta and Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) are bracing for information requests, future congressional hearings, and potential subpoenas. Congress is expected to shift its scrutiny toward businesses if the Trump administration resists congressional information requests, as companies have less flexibility to refuse lawmakers’ demands, according to the report.

Meta Platforms, Paramount, Kalshi and Palantir did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comments.

Midterm Jitters for GOP

The report comes as Republicans face a challenging midterm election, with current forecasts giving Democrats an edge in the House. The Senate race is also considered highly competitive.

President Trump said MAGA Inc. plans to deploy a large share of its roughly $850 million war chest to support Republican candidates ahead of the midterms. Trump said he would use much of the money, along with some of his own funds, to support strong Republican candidates, adding that the party is in a strong position.

Meanwhile, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries vowed to “hold every single member of the Trump cartel accountable” if Democrats win the House in November. This includes companies that have made large donations to Trump or his projects, and those connected to Trump’s family members or the children of the president’s senior aides.

Coinbase Defends Trump Ballroom Donation

In November, Coinbase Global Inc. (NASDAQ: COIN) COO Emilie Choi defended the company’s donation to Trump’s ballroom project, acknowledging it was partly intended to maintain good relations with the White House. She saw no issue with the contribution, arguing that private industry funding upgrades to government buildings is simply a reality.

The list of donors for the Ballroom project released by the White House included major corporations such as Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Apple, Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) and Palantir. Coinbase, along with Tether (CRYPTO: USDT) and Ripple (CRYPTO: XRP), were among the donors from the crypto industry.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) has reportedly temporarily paused its financing program that offered credit support to AI cloud providers in exchange for a share of their revenue, backing away from the initiative less than two months after unveiling it.

Employees Raise Antitrust Concerns

Some of the company’s employees told current and potential customers they were worried the program could draw antitrust scrutiny, citing sensitivities around how much control the chip giant could exert over its customers’ businesses, The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.

Nvidia stepped back from the program last week and could revamp it in the future or fold it into a different initiative, the report added, citing people familiar with the matter.

“The new business model we introduced in July that opens up compute access to the fast-growing AI ecosystem is still in place and continues to evolve due to high demand,” an Nvidia spokesperson told Benzinga.

The Program Launched In July

The initiative was introduced in July, offering AI cloud providers credit support through minimum revenue guarantees in exchange for a share of future revenue above a specified threshold, allowing the company to profit from both hardware sales and a cut of customer earnings.

“In this model, we get paid twice, once on the hardware sale and again through the share of rental revenue,” CFO Colette Kress said on Wednesday’s second-quarter earnings call.

She pushed back against claims that the arrangement amounts to “circular financing,” saying the company’s risk remains low because its computing hardware can always be redeployed to other customers.

Part of a Broader Financing Push

The revenue-sharing model is one of several tools Nvidia has used to support its customer ecosystem, including a nearly $50 billion investment in frontier AI labs and a partnership with Apollo Global Management (NYSE: APO), BlackRock Inc. (NYSE: BLK), Blackstone Inc. (NYSE: BX), Brookfield Asset Management (NYSE: BAM), Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) and KKR & Co. Inc. (NYSE: KKR) to mobilize more than $500 billion in third-party infrastructure capital.

Earlier this month, “The Big Short” investor Michael Burry called Nvidia’s AI financing push a “Wall Street stunt.”

The pause comes even as Nvidia posted record second-quarter revenue of $96.22 billion, above the $92.11 billion analysts expected, according to Benzinga Pro, and guided for $108 billion in the third quarter, a figure that would mark roughly 1,730% revenue growth over four years if achieved.

Marvell Technology, Inc (NASDAQ:MRVL) shares fell nearly 8% in Friday premarket trading as investors reset expectations after the company’s earnings report, despite continued data center strength and a stronger growth outlook.

Marvell Beats Q2 Estimates, Raises Growth Expectations

Marvell reported second-quarter revenue of $2.74 billion and adjusted EPS of 94 cents, both beating the consensus estimates.

Management pointed to continued strength across its Data Center portfolio. For the third quarter, Marvell guided revenue to $3.15 billion, plus or minus 5%, and adjusted EPS to $1.10, plus or minus 5 cents.

The company also expects an adjusted gross margin of 57.5% to 58.5%.

CEO Matt Murphy raised Marvell’s revenue target for next year to roughly $18 billion, implying about 50% growth.

Google Deal Clarification Cools Investor Enthusiasm

CNBC noted that Marvell’s data center business is growing more than 60%, supported by optical components that connect AI servers and custom chips, which Murphy expects to more than double.

However, Murphy said revenue from Marvell’s recently announced Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) Google warrant agreement is already included in next year’s projections.

That clarification reduced some investor enthusiasm because Wall Street had viewed the Google agreement as additional upside beyond existing expectations. Murphy said the larger contribution from the deal should come the following year.

CNBC also pointed to elevated expectations after Marvell shares had climbed about 184% year to date and nearly 30% over the previous month.

Seymour Prefers NVIDIA At Current Valuations

Seymour Asset Management founder and CIO Tim Seymour said Marvell sits in attractive areas of the AI infrastructure market, particularly networking and data centers.

He called Marvell’s forward guidance strong but said investors still face uncertainty over the appropriate valuation multiple for the stock.

Seymour does not own Marvell and said he would rather own NVIDIA Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) at what he considers a more attractive valuation.

While September carries a longstanding reputation as the “worst month of the year” for the S&P 500, Carson Group Chief Market Strategist Ryan Detrick argued that the market’s strong year-to-date trajectory suggests 2026 could defy those historical odds.

Historical Odds Favor the Bulls

Seasonal anxiety often peaks as September begins, but Detrick highlights that historical trends tell a far more optimistic story when equities enter the month on solid footing. Taking to X, Detrick acknowledged the seasonal reputation of September while pointing out key historical exceptions during strong market years.

“Yes, September is historically the worst month of the year. Get ready to hear that a lot next week,” Detrick posted. “But things do pretty well when August is green and the year is off to a solid start (up between 10% and 17.5%).”

Historical data stretching back to World War II reveals that when the S&P 500 achieves a positive August alongside year-to-date gains between 10% and 17.5%, a scenario matching 2026’s 3% August gain so far and 12.8% YTD return, September itself averages a 1.0% gain.

More importantly, the final four months of the year have closed higher 10 out of 11 times, generating an average return of 5.6%.

Key Technical Levels and Seasonality

Speaking on an episode of the Facts Versus Feelings podcast, Detrick noted that seasonal turbulence remains possible, particularly given broader political and election-year dynamics. “August and September historically in a midterm year can be trouble, can be volatile,” Detrick admitted.

However, Detrick maintains that strong internal market breadth and technical support levels bode well for investors. He specifically highlighted 7,610, the S&P 500’s June 2 peak, as a vital floor.

“Previous peaks or previous resistance should be new support,” Detrick noted, adding that as long as the index stays above 7,610, the broader technical structure remains net optimistic.

With history and market internals on the side of the bulls, Detrick urges investors not to panic over calendar-based fears.

After the stellar 2010s, the bond market performance has been disappointing in the 2020s. According to technical analyst Francis Hunt, this post-2020 rout marks the end of a 40-year debt bull market.

In his view, sovereigns and large institutions are increasingly forced to preserve capital in hard assets rather than chase paper gains.

Debt Cycle Is Rolling Over

For Hunt, the global financial system has moved past the easy-money era that began in the early 1980s. Since the 2020 bond-market capitulation, he argues in a recent interview, yields have entered a structural reversal marked by "ever lower highs and ever lower lows" in debt prices and an eventual nominal devaluation of the instruments themselves.

Furthermore, the shift has, in his opinion, changed how investors should read headline gains in equities and other risk assets. What looks like growth in index levels is, in large part, the denominator effect of weakening fiat purchasing power.

"It’s not the same dollar anymore," he remarked. In such an environment, nominal wealth expands, while real wealth contracts. For Hunt, that dynamic makes gold the pressure valve.

"The debt crisis is the turbo juice for gold," he remarked, arguing that capital starts prioritizing preservation over return. Investors stop asking what can compound the fastest, and start asking what can’t be printed, diluted, or blocked.

The "Hotel California" Liquidity Regime

The treasury market, in Hunt’s view, is a one-way architecture – an easy entry, but constrained exit. "You can check out any time you like, but you can never leave," he said, recalling the evergreen lyrics.

Instead of outright liquidation, creditors are pushed toward swap lines, repo facilities and borrowing against the collateral they already own. That creates what Hunt sees as a manufactured asymmetry: buyers are welcome, sellers are constrained.

He cites U.K.’s 2022 liability-driven crisis, strains at the California State Teachers’ Retirement System, and recent pressure on Gulf states in the aftermath of an Iran war. In each case, the system responded by constraining liquidation and extending liquidity against pledged assets.

Japan as the Pressure Point

Yet Japan might be the most important test case. With over $1.1 trillion in U.S. Treasuries, it’s large enough to matter and constrained enough to be trapped.

Rather than selling freely, he said, Japanese holders are effectively offered limited borrowing capacity against their bonds — "at the moment we’re allowing 60 billion," he said, pointing at the discrepancy compared to the size of the stockpile.

A deeper rupture, he warns, could force a violent unwind in the carry trade. It would drag the capital out of global risk assets and push Treasury yields higher- something the US cannot afford.

That scenario would invert the standard textbook logic where higher yields attract durable inflows. In sovereign stress, Hunt says, yield can look less like reward and more like risk premium.

Gold in the Real Denominator

Hunt’s chart work centers on measuring equities against gold rather than against the dollar. In that frame, he says, U.S. stocks peaked in 1999, staged a secondary high in 2021 and now look vulnerable to a longer secular reset.

SPY divided by Gold, 3-Month chart, Source: TradingView

In Hunt’s view, the technical line in the sand is around 0.15. A break of that neckline would signal a potential rapid move in gold against the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY).

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq may still grind higher in nominal terms, he argues, but that is because the benchmark currency is being debased at the same time. Gold, by contrast, captures the loss of confidence in paper claims.

"We are entering a far more convex period," he said, borrowing Ernest Hemingway’s line that bankruptcy happens "slowly at first, and then suddenly."

NVIDIA Corp’s (NASDAQ:NVDA) reported $13 billion pursuit of Hugging Face could give the chipmaker deeper control over how AI models are discovered, developed and deployed across the broader ecosystem.

• NVIDIA stock is showing positive momentum. What’s the outlook for NVDA shares?

Shah Sees Hugging Face Expanding Nvidia’s AI Reach

Counterpoint Research analyst Neil Shah said on Thursday that the potential acquisition represents a broader horizontal integration strategy for Nvidia.

Hugging Face has become a central platform where developers publish, rank, fine-tune and deploy AI models.

Shah believes ownership could give Nvidia earlier visibility into which models, architectures, compression techniques and agent frameworks are gaining traction before that demand reaches the chip market.

He said that information could help Nvidia shape its compilers, runtimes and future systems while pulling more workloads toward its silicon, software and infrastructure.

Open Models and Physical AI Could Strengthen Nvidia’s Position

Shah sees open models as an important motivation behind the potential acquisition.

While closed AI labs increasingly develop their own chips, Nvidia serves a much broader range of models and could use Hugging Face to make open-model deployment faster and more efficient on its hardware.

He also highlighted robotics and world models as fast-growing areas on Hugging Face.

Shah believes Nvidia could use the platform to strengthen distribution for its Physical AI technologies, including Nemotron and Alpamayo.

Neutrality Remains the Key Risk

Shah said Hugging Face’s value depends heavily on remaining neutral because major AI labs, startups and Nvidia hardware competitors all publish models on the platform.

He warned that the platform could lose value if developers begin viewing it as too closely tied to Nvidia or CUDA.

In his view, the deal works best if Nvidia keeps Hugging Face open to competitors while using its broad developer reach to encourage more open models, AI agents and robotics workloads to run on Nvidia systems.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang says securing power for AI data centers can take years, even as demand for the company’s chips continues to outrun supply.

Evercore ISI says that could create an opportunity for Bloom Energy Corp. (NYSE:BE), whose onsite fuel cells are designed to get data centers running without waiting years for new grid connections.

Huang told investors Wednesday that building an AI factory now requires companies to “secure the land, power, and shell,” a process that he said can take two to three years.

The bullish call comes with Bloom shares still roughly 38% below their $351.28 52-week high.

Evercore Sees Bloom Benefiting

Evercore analyst Nicholas Amicucci said Nvidia’s outlook suggests AI compute demand is running ahead of the physical infrastructure needed to support it.

He identified Bloom, Constellation Energy, Talen Energy, NRG Energy and American Electric Power as potential beneficiaries as Nvidia pushes further into solving the power problem.

Nvidia is already putting money behind that effort. The company this month agreed to provide credit support for the first 4.25 gigawatts of land, power and shell capacity at SB Energy’s Ohio data-center campus and invested $1.5 billion in the developer.

Evercore has an Outperform rating and $350 price target on Bloom, among the more bullish calls on Wall Street. The stock closed Thursday at $217.83.

Prediction markets are also pricing continued growth in the number of U.S. data centers.

Kalshi traders give a 66% chance the count reaches at least 5,300 by the end of 2026. The odds of at least 5,400 stand at 52%, while 5,500 or more trades at 45%. Data Center Map, the source used to settle the Kalshi market, currently lists 4,767 U.S. facilities.

That expansion could put further pressure on the power infrastructure Nvidia says is already struggling to keep pace with AI demand.

Kalshi and Benzinga have an existing data collaboration agreement.

Bloom Pitches a Faster Route to Power

Bloom says its first system under a broader Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL) partnership became fully operational in just 55 days. Oracle has contracted an initial 1.2 GW of Bloom capacity, with an agreement allowing it to procure up to 2.8 GW.f

That is far faster than the two-to-three-year infrastructure timelines Huang described.

Project Jupiter shows the potential scale. Oracle and BorderPlex Digital Assets said the New Mexico campus could use up to 2.45 GW of Bloom fuel cells, with the infrastructure intended to serve OpenAI.

The project also highlights the risks. The New Mexico Supreme Court on Sunday temporarily froze both the air-quality permit proceeding for Jupiter’s microgrid and an emergency authorization allowing water from a new well for construction.

Responses are due Sep. 2, while an air-permit hearing had been scheduled for Sep. 14.

Bloom also faces a proposed securities class action alleging it misled investors about its reliance on Chinese-sourced scandium. The company has rejected the claims, saying its scandium supply is not dependent on China.

Bloom reported second-quarter revenue of $1.07 billion, up 165.5% year over year, and raised its 2026 revenue outlook to $3.9 billion to $4.2 billion.

Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) is already running AI workloads on IREN’s infrastructure. NVIDIA Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) has now validated another layer of its platform. But according to co-CEO Daniel Roberts, those milestones point to a bigger story: in the AI infrastructure race, owning the entire stack — not just the chips — could become the industry’s defining advantage.

• IREN shares are sliding. What’s weighing on IREN shares?

Speaking on IREN’s fiscal 2026 earnings call, Roberts argued that the company’s strategy extends far beyond acquiring Nvidia GPUs. Instead, he said IREN is building a vertically integrated AI infrastructure platform spanning power, data centers, compute and software — an approach he believes creates more value than relying on third-party providers for critical pieces of the stack.

Microsoft and Nvidia Reinforce IREN’s AI Stack Strategy

IREN highlighted a series of milestones that underscore that strategy.

The company said Horizon 1 — the first of four planned 50-megawatt AI cloud deployments under its Microsoft contract — was delivered during the quarter. Roberts also noted that the company’s 2026 contracted annual recurring revenue has reached $4 billion, with $1 billion already operational, while another $700 million of ARR tied to its Nvidia Cloud contract is expected to ramp in 2027.

On the software side, Roberts pointed to another milestone announced alongside the earnings release.

“Just today, Mirantis was named an inaugural Nvidia Certified Hypervisor. So we’ve now got Nvidia validation at the software layer as well as the hardware.”

Mirantis, which IREN recently acquired, enables the company to offer managed AI cloud services alongside bare-metal GPU infrastructure, expanding the range of customers it can serve.

Read Also: IREN CEO: AI Buildout Is 'Permanent Whack-A-Mole' — And That's The Real Bottleneck

IREN CEO Says Owning Every Layer Creates More Value

For Roberts, the Microsoft deployment and Nvidia software certification illustrate a broader investment thesis rather than isolated achievements.

“Why own all three?” he asked, referring to infrastructure, GPUs and software.

“Because each layer makes the one underneath it worth more. A grid connection is worth more with a data center on it. Worth more again with GPUs inside. More again with services wrapped around the customer.”

He contrasted IREN’s approach with much of the broader AI infrastructure market.

“Most of this market rents at least one of those layers; we own the entire stack.”

Management argued that vertical integration gives IREN greater flexibility to serve different customer types, from hyperscalers seeking bare-metal GPU clusters to enterprise AI developers that require managed cloud services and orchestration software.

The Mirantis acquisition also opens the door to new offerings such as on-demand AI compute and managed services, complementing the company’s long-term cloud infrastructure contracts.

What Investors Should Watch

The AI infrastructure story has largely centered on access to Nvidia’s latest chips. IREN’s latest earnings call suggests management believes the competitive landscape is shifting toward a broader question: who owns the infrastructure surrounding those GPUs.

That thesis is now supported by tangible milestones. Microsoft has begun taking delivery under its AI cloud agreement, Nvidia has validated IREN’s software layer through Mirantis, and management says each additional layer strengthens the economics of the one below it.

For investors, the next test will be whether that vertically integrated model translates into sustained customer growth, expanding margins and higher-value AI cloud contracts as demand continues to scale.

Whitney Tilson on NVDA Stock

Nvidia reported second-quarter results that beat analyst estimates, but it was its early 2028 unofficial guidance that stole the spotlight during the conference call.

"There’s no sign of a slowdown in demand for its chips, which are at the heart of the AI-infrastructure boom, former hedge fund manager Whitney Tilson said in a blog this week.

Tilson said the second-quarter revenue and earnings per share figures beat estimates, but were far from being "blowout numbers."

The market expert highlighted the guidance for revenue growth of 70% in fiscal 2028, calling it "staggering." Nvidia said the guidance would be more than 100% year-over-year revenue growth if not for supply constraints.

Tilson highlights some writings from market experts that share some of the negatives from Nvidia’s earnings report and conference call. This includes lower gross margin guidance and supply-chain commitments.

On the subject of supply-chain commitments, Tilson is cautious that the company’s strategy and growing commitments could "end poorly for Nvidia" if the AI bubble bursts. A report from the Wall Street Journal says that the company in the middle (Nvidia) can have supply chain commitments as insurance and a strategic advantage, but it can turn into a "painful liability."

The Wall Street Journal compares the potential liabilities to Cisco Systems in 2001, with the company on the hook for commitments to suppliers when the dot-com bubble burst.

Tilson says one of the biggest risks for Nvidia is if OpenAI blows up, a move that "would roil the entire sector.

"I think this is likely," Tilson said.

Tilson wrote more about a potential AI bubble burst earlier this week.

Read Also: Dan Ives: Nvidia Earnings Should 'Hang in the Louvre,' US Takes Lead Over China 'For First Time in 30 Years'

Buy or Sell Nvidia Stock Today?

So what are Nvidia investors left to do with the stock while there is a possibility of an AI bubble bursting and the company being hurt by its growing supply commitment strategy?

Tilson says Nvidia stock is currently cheap based on trading at around 25 times current-year earnings per share and around 17 times next year’s estimated earnings per share.

"These are very low multiples for a company this dominant, profitable and fast-growing. And if Nvidia hits its projected revenue numbers, earnings will be much higher than analyst expectations — and the stock could double in the next year or two. But that’s a big ‘if,’" Tilson said.

Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang is pushing back on Bill Gates‘ warning that artificial intelligence could permanently wipe out huge numbers of jobs, arguing the technology will instead be a net job creator “at a scale that we’ve never seen.”

“I love the heck out of Bill,” Huang told Fox Business this week. “But I don’t see what he sees.”

Huang acknowledged some jobs will disappear, but argued Gates is drawing the wrong conclusion about what happens next.

What Gates Sees

Gates argued in an essay this week that AI differs from past technological revolutions because it can replace human cognitive labor itself rather than simply making workers more productive.

He expects entry-level and mid-level roles to be hit first, including customer support, software engineering and paralegal work, before increasingly capable robots threaten physical jobs.

To slow displacement, Gates has proposed taxing AI tokens and robots and using the money to fund retraining and a stronger safety net.

Huang Sees the Opposite Feedback Loop

Huang’s economics run the other way. AI makes workers more productive, higher productivity boosts profits, and ambitious companies reinvest those profits to expand and hire.

“Some jobs will be eliminated,” Huang said, but “many new jobs will be created.”

Gates sees substitution. Huang sees expansion.

So Far, No AI Jobs Apocalypse

The labor market has so far given both men some ammunition. AI was cited in 112,713 announced U.S. job cuts through July, roughly 24% of all cuts, and has ranked as the leading stated reason for layoffs for five consecutive months, according to a Challenger, Gray & Christmas report.

Yet total announced cuts are down 41% from the same period last year, and July’s tally was the lowest monthly total in two years. AI-related layoffs are clearly real. A broad AI-driven employment collapse is not.

But Gates May Have Found the Canary

The more worrying evidence sits with young workers. Stanford researchers using payroll data covering millions of workers found employment among 22-to-25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers.

The adjustment appears to be coming mainly through reduced hiring rather than firings, and the authors caution the results are not proof AI caused the decline.

The first sign of AI displacement may not be mass layoffs. It may be companies simply hiring fewer people at the bottom of the ladder.

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction markets aren’t pricing a broad employment shock, at least for now.

Polymarket traders price only an 11% chance the U.S. unemployment rate, which stood at 4.1% in July, reaches 5% this year. The market sees little sign of the sharp economy-wide rise in unemployment Gates fears.

For now, the evidence sits somewhere between the two billionaires: AI is already eliminating some jobs and appears to be squeezing entry-level hiring, but the economy-wide employment destruction Gates fears has yet to materialize.

In his first symposium keynote as Fed Chair, Kevin Warsh said summer’s softer inflation prints failed to convince him that underlying trends have improved.

Policymakers must be confident inflation is returning to 2% “clearly and at sufficient speed,” he warned. “Otherwise, we have work to do.”

He refused to call that forward guidance. The rates market called it for him.

Odds of a quarter-point hike at the Sept. 15–16 meeting jumped to 59.7% by late morning, up from 35.4% Thursday and 39.9% last week, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.

The two-year Treasury yield rose 9 basis points to 4.32%, a one-month high.

The real signal, however, lies in the yield curve rather than the front end.

While the two-year spiked, the 30-year yield held flat at 5.19% and the 10-year rose less than 4 basis points to 4.71%. That classic bear flattener shows traders pricing in short-term Fed tightening—and betting it will successfully keep long-term inflation in check.

Traders believe Warsh will hike, and that the hikes will work. That is why equities escaped the damage.

Bitcoin, Gold Sink

The S&P 500 traded near 7,724, down 0.09%, the Nasdaq 100 slipped 0.24%. The dollar index rose 0.4% to 99.57.

The pain concentrated in the two positions that had run hardest into the speech.

Spot gold fell 1.7% to roughly $4,526 an ounce. SPDR Gold Shares (NYSE:GLD) dropped 1.8% and VanEck Gold Miners ETF (NYSE:GDX) fell 2.7%.

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) slid to about $78,100 after clearing $80,000 earlier this week, with iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (NASDAQ:IBIT) off 2.5%.

Two Trades, Same Assumption

Bitcoin ran from roughly $64,000 to $80,000 this month after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent doubled long-dated buyback operations to at least $4 billion apiece starting Sept. 9, and gold rallied alongside it.

Markets had spent August betting on a Fed holding steady in September.

That is the assumption that got repriced on Friday.

Two prints now stand between here and the Sept. 16 decision: August payrolls and August CPI.

A 60% chance is not a done deal. Those numbers determine whether it becomes one.

NVIDIA Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) stock is up 18% year-to-date in 2026, with shares trading higher this week after the company reported second-quarter financial results and updated guidance. While the stock is gaining value in 2026, another Nvidia item is also seeing increased valuation: autographs from CEO Jensen Huang.

Jensen Huang Autograph Up for Auction

One of the richest people in the world, Nvidia co-founder and CEO Huang has grown into one of the most recognizable figures in the investment world and among the technology sector, often referenced as the "Godfather of AI."

Fans of Huang and Nvidia are likely among the bidders on Nvidia- and Huang-related memorabilia that has come up for auction this year, including a worn leather jacket from Huang.

Currently up for auction as part of the "Fine autographs and artifacts" auction from RR Auction is a twice-signed Nvidia GeForce RTX 5080 Graphics Card.

The item features Huang’s signature in black ink on the packaging and a signature in gold ink on the metal housing of the card. The auction includes original packaging and the original shipping box.

Set to close on Sept. 16, the auction has a current high bid of $517. RR Auction estimates the closing price will be $3,000 or more.

For context, this means you could buy 14 shares of Nvidia for around $3,000 or buy this one-of-a-kind memorabilia piece, assuming it doesn’t go much higher than the auction house estimate.

Huang’s autograph is one of over 600 signed pieces in the latest RR Auction, with autographs from The Beatles, Harper Lee, Abraham Lincoln, Bruce Lee and John Hancock also featured.

Read Also: Nvidia Stock at Crossroads: Expert Says Shares ‘Could Double’ or AI Bubble Could Pop

Recent Jensen Huang Auctions

As mentioned above, the auction house estimate is $3,000 for the twice-signed Huang Nvidia graphics card, but there is a good chance the final price ends higher based on recent history.

In June, a signed Huang trading card sold for $1,836 versus a $1,000 pre-auction estimate.

In July, Sotheby’s auctioned an iconic Tom Ford leather jacket worn by Huang. The jacket had an auction house estimate of $40,000 to $60,000, but ended up sold for a winning bid of $960,000.

On RR Auction, there were several Huang pieces sold earlier this month, including a Huang-autographed picture sold for $1,169, easily beating the $400 pre-auction estimate, and a twice-signed RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell that sold for $57,450, significantly higher than the $6,000 estimate.

Earlier this year, a twice-signed GeForce RTX 5090 Founders Edition GPU sold for $10,005 in March via RR Auction, beating a pre-auction estimate of $8,000.

Huang-signed merchandise and Nvidia memorabilia are in a market that is heating up, and the latest auction could show if demand is still there with Nvidia the most valuable company in the world.

OpenAI has also been building out its footprint across Asia-Pacific, with offices opened over the past two years in cities including Singapore, Tokyo, Seoul, Sydney, Delhi and Tokyo.

Two weeks ago, OpenAI replaced Chief Revenue Officer Denise Dresser, who was in the role for about eight months. Dali Rajic was named in her place, with the company framing the hire as preparing for a new wave of models it expects to reshape how organizations operate.

Two days before Dresser’s departure was announced, OpenAI also lost longtime executive Brad Lightcap, who had served as chief operating officer. Lightcap said he would be “starting something new,” without sharing details.

About a month earlier, OpenAI Product and Business Chief Fidji Simo stepped down to address a “chronic illness,” although she continues to advise the company.

OpenAI may be pushing back its public debut as it weighs whether market conditions can support its reported goal of a $1 trillion valuation.
